correctness.rationale: Using published geometric theorems on the DGZ curve, the only short automorphism orbits are contained in extensions of degrees 2 and 3, with no base-field points. A seventh-extension point therefore lies in a free orbit of size |G|. Frobenius commutes with G, and if it fixes that orbit it must act by right translation of order dividing 7. As 7 does not divide |G| for all six q, the orbit must instead belong to a 7-cycle of free orbits; N7>=7|G|. Exact integer Hasse–Weil bounds computed from the published genus give N7<=U(q)<7|G| for each of q=3,5,17,19,31,47. The proof is not extrapolated from tests; it uses only established group-action results, elementary group theory, and Hasse–Weil. All nonstandard premises were inspected in the source text.

claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The union of the two published short orbits and their degree-1–6 counts does not determine N7. Using that both Frobenius and G act on the same free orbit, and that 7 does not divide |G|, introduces the extra sevenfold orbit packet and produces a contradiction. Thus the stated result is not an implication of the published numerical formulas without the additional argument.

originality.rationale: Primary DGZ literature establishes N1–N3 (2018) and N4–N6 (2022); it does not give these six N7 counts. Group-orbit plus Hasse–Weil estimates on a single long orbit do not imply the new result; the sevenfold Frobenius-packet obstruction provides the missing strict lower bound. Actual published-finding corpus and public source searches, including aliases and degree-seven equivalents, found no covering statement. Remaining unindexed-priority risk is disclosed.
residual_risks: The general right-translation argument is elementary; similar degree-seven applications might exist under another title or in unindexed finite-field literature.
The recent literature search is not exhaustive, so novelty is a best-knowledge assessment rather than a certification.

value.rationale: The first post-N6 extension degree is a mathematically motivated gap in the point spectrum of a canonical very-high-automorphism curve. The result gives exact, surprising point absence for six concrete and naturally determined finite fields, with a structural mechanism not recoverable from bare group orbit size estimates. This constrains the zeta-function coefficients and the possible degrees of closed points. The finite cutoff is selected by the natural arithmetic inequalities, not by an arbitrary subfamily.
